outcome: No new proof, disproof or case of the bullet's representation-side statement (values at 1 of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of a finite Weyl group giving multiplicities for complex semisimple Lie groups and algebras) appeared since 26 January 2024; the statement was proved in 1981 (Beilinson–Bernstein and Brylinski–Kashiwara), and the in-window events found are analogues (quantum, modular, p-adic, finite-group, infinite-rank, stable-parabolic), combinatorial and matroid results on neighbouring quantities, and two AI-credited pieces of work on those neighbouring objects.
problem_asks: Read from the statement alone, part by part: (1) the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures, plural as the bullet words them. (2) The quantity: the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of a finite Weyl group, indexed by pairs of elements (y, w), evaluated at 1, i.e. P_{y,w}(1). (3) The setting: complex semisimple Lie groups and Lie algebras, which the statement puts in characteristic 0 and finite-dimensional semisimple terms; the statement does not mention Kac–Moody, super, quantum, modular or p-adic cases. (4) The relation asserted: those values are tied to 'representations' of the groups and algebras. The sources identify this as the composition (Jordan–Hölder) multiplicities of simple highest-weight modules in Verma modules in category O. (5) Groups and algebras: the bullet names both complex semisimple Lie groups and Lie algebras, while the 1979 formulation and the 1981 proofs as I read them are stated for Lie algebras (category O); the group-level reading is a part I did not verify separately. (6) Plural 'conjectures': the 1979 paper put forth two conjectures which the linked Wikipedia article calls equivalent (the representation-side character formula and the positivity of the coefficients of P_{y,w}); the bullet's wording names only the representation side, so positivity is recorded here as the companion conjecture, not as a named part. (7) The bullet does not state whether integral/regular or singular/non-integral weights are included; I did not establish what the 1981 proofs cover on this point.

events.what_happened: Alexander Beilinson and Joseph Bernstein announced a proof of the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures (and of the Jantzen conjectures) in 1981, in the note “Localisation de g-modules” (C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. I, 1981), by localisation of g-modules as sheaves of twisted differential operators on the flag variety. The Wikipedia article (fetched) cites it for the 1981 proof over characteristic-0 algebraically closed fields. A search snippet describes the 1981 note as a sketch; I did not open the note. The complete Jantzen-conjecture write-up is a separate 1993 Beilinson–Bernstein paper, which I did not open.
events.revisions: Full Jantzen-conjecture proof: Beilinson–Bernstein, “A proof of Jantzen conjectures” (Gelfand Seminar, 1993), cited via a search snippet, not opened.
events.delivers: Establishes the 1979 character statement for complex semisimple Lie algebras in characteristic 0: the values at 1 of the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials give the composition multiplicities of simple highest-weight modules in Verma modules. Restrictions I could not confirm from the note: whether it covers all weights or only the regular integral case, and whether it addresses the group wording of the bullet.
events.remains: On the sources' account, nothing of the representation-side statement is left open. Unverified: the group-level wording and the scope of weights.

events.direction: Confirms the conjectured relation: the Kazhdan–Lusztig values at 1 are the multiplicities, as conjectured.

events.what_happened: Xiaoyu Chen and HongSheng Hu, “Boundedness of Lusztig's a-function for Coxeter groups of finite rank”, arXiv:2503.06432 (v1 9 March 2025; latest v10 24 September 2026). The arXiv page gives a journal DOI 10.1007/s00222-026-01453-1, with the prefix used by Inventiones Mathematicae; the two venue claims conflict.

The a-function is a quantity in the cell theory of the Hecke algebra, not the values at 1 as representation multiplicities for complex Lie groups. The claimed consequence (P1–P15 in the equal-parameter case) is reported by the news piece, not in the arXiv abstract.

events.what_happened: Grant T. Barkley, Christian Gaetz and Thomas Lam, arXiv:2601.07793 (v1 12 January 2026; v2 24 February 2026). The abstract (fetched) says they prove the combinatorial invariance of the coefficient of q in Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials for arbitrary Coxeter groups; obtain the Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture, of Lusztig and of Dyer, for Bruhat intervals of length at most 6; prove the Gabber–Joseph conjecture for the second-highest Ext group of a pair of Verma modules; and prove combinatorial invariance of the dimension of that Ext group and of the numbers of frozen and mutable variables in a cluster structure on Richardson varieties.
events.delivers: Combinatorial invariance of the q-coefficient for arbitrary Coxeter groups; CIC for intervals of length at most 6; and a result on the second-highest Ext group between Verma modules (Gabber–Joseph). The Ext result touches category O for complex semisimple Lie algebras, but it concerns Ext dimensions and the coefficient of q, not the value at 1 that the bullet asks for, so it is a changed quantity on the representation side.
events.remains: The bullet's composition-multiplicity relation at q = 1 for the general case. The Ext2 result does not give that relation for all Verma pairs, on the abstract's account.

events.direction: Does not settle the composition-multiplicity relation. Adjacent: an Ext result for Verma modules in category O, which a judging pass may read as touching the representation side.

events.what_happened: Ronnie Cheng and Shurui Liu, “Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of matroids need not be unimodal”, arXiv:2607.24186 (v1 27 July 2026; v2 28 July 2026). The abstract (fetched) says they construct representable matroids over every finite field whose Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials are not unimodal, so the conjectures that these polynomials are log-concave and real-rooted are false. The appendix (fetched via the fetch tool; the text returned is a paraphrase-style summary, not checked verbatim) says the motivating counterexample was first produced by the automated mathematical reasoning agent Rethlas, run with GPT-5.6 Sol as the base model at reasoning effort max, taking 4 h 59 min to a solution the Rethlas verifier accepted; the same problem given to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra through its web interface 'failed to give a complete solution' across two prompts. Appendix §A.3 says the verifier rejected an earlier version for a missing spanning hypothesis, which Rethlas then added. The acknowledgements say a human 'kindly helped with the experiments'.
events.delivers: Counterexamples to unimodality, log-concavity and real-rootedness of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of representable matroids over finite fields. Matroid Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, not the Lie-theoretic polynomials of the bullet; a different question.

disputes.summary: Attribution of the 1981 independent proofs is inconsistent across sources. The Wikipedia KL-polynomial article and the Losev lecture (search snippet) credit Beilinson–Bernstein and Brylinski–Kashiwara; an nLab entry (search snippet, not opened) credits the proof to Borho–Brylinski and Masaki Kashiwara. Not resolved here.

The conjecture number of the ChatGPT-generated proof in arXiv:2412.01283 is inconsistent across reads: Remark 6.5 refers to Conjecture 6.4 (fetched excerpt), while one read of the acknowledgements and a search snippet give 6.1. Model naming for that proof comes only from the fetch tool's excerpt of the remark.

summary: The bullet is the 1979 Kazhdan–Lusztig character conjecture: the values at 1 of the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of a finite Weyl group give the composition multiplicities of simple highest-weight modules in Verma modules, for complex semisimple Lie algebras (category O). The bullet appears in Wikipedia's list under Algebra / Representation theory, and the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial article it links to (fetched) says the two conjectures put forth in 1979 were 'proved over characteristic 0 algebraically closed fields independently' by Beilinson–Bernstein and by Brylinski–Kashiwara in 1981, and that they are 'known to be equivalent'. Those 1981 proofs are the solution events; I did not open the primary papers, so their scope (all weights or regular integral only; Lie algebras versus the group wording of the bullet) is not verified. Later proofs of the same statement predate the window: Elias–Williamson (arXiv December 2012, Annals 2014; abstract says 'Using results of Soergel one may deduce an algebraic proof of the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture') and Braverman–Finkelberg–Nakajima (arXiv July 2020, Crelle 2022; geometric via zastava spaces). I found no in-window paper that changes the bullet's statement. The in-window work I opened is adjacent: quantum (Tanisaki 2021 preprint, with later versions per a snippet), finite groups (Bezrukavnikov et al., February 2025, whose abstract weakened between v1 and v2), char-p modular (Riche–Situ, November 2025, conditional on Lusztig's conjecture), p-adic (Balodis, October 2025), sl_∞ Koszulity (Creedon–Mazorchuk, April 2025), stable and complex-rank parabolic (Wan, December 2025), combinatorial invariance and the coefficient of q (Barkley–Gaetz April 2024; Barkley–Gaetz–Lam January 2026, which touches an Ext group between Verma modules, a changed quantity), Lusztig's a-function (Chen–Hu, March 2025; a news report says published September 2026 with P1–P15 consequence, and the venue conflicts), and matroid Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials (Cheng–Liu July 2026; Badalov September 2026). On AI: no event on the bullet's own statement names an AI system; the 1981, 2012 and 2020 proofs name none in what I read (abstract-level for the last two). The AI-credited items are all on neighbouring objects: ChatGPT in Lacabanne–Tubbenhauer–Vaz (acknowledgements; a ChatGPT 5.5 Pro proof remark dated to a June 2026 contact), Rethlas with GPT-5.6 Sol in Cheng–Liu (the appendix, read through the fetch tool), OpenAI Codex with GPT-6 Astra in Badalov, and unnamed 'machine learning models' behind the 2021 Blundell et al. formula for symmetric groups, whose conjecture a 2025 seminar abstract credits to 'Google DeepMind' with 'machine learning techniques'. Close calls: (i) the 1979 pair includes positivity, which Elias–Williamson extended to all Coxeter groups; the bullet names only the representation side, but the linked article calls the two conjectures equivalent, so a judging pass has to decide whether positivity is part of the bullet; (ii) whether a result for Lie algebras answers the group wording of the bullet; (iii) whether the 1981 proofs cover all weights. The Wikipedia list still includes the bullet although the article it links records the 1981 proof, so the bullet appears stale.
competing_reading: Read the bullet broadly as the family of Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures: positivity (settled for all Coxeter groups by Elias–Williamson, pre-window), Lusztig's modular, quantum and finite-group versions (open in general, with in-window partial results), and the P1–P15 cell conjectures (Chen–Hu, with a reported in-window consequence). On that reading, in-window progress exists, including Bezrukavnikov et al., Chen–Hu and Barkley–Gaetz–Lam, and the AI-credited work becomes relevant. Read narrowly, as the list's wording 'relating the values at 1 ... with representations of complex semisimple Lie groups and Lie algebras' most naturally does, the statement was settled in 1981 and nothing in-window touches it. The record's events support the narrow reading for the representation side, and the broad reading only through neighbouring objects.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The 1981 Beilinson–Bernstein note and Brylinski–Kashiwara paper, to confirm whether they cover all weights, the group-level wording, and the exact claim. (2) The Wikipedia list's history or talk page, to see why the bullet is listed and whether the editors meant a narrower open part. (3) Full text of Gabber–Joseph 1981, which is not read here. (4) Verbatim text of the Cheng–Liu appendix and of Remark 6.5 in arXiv:2412.01283 (both read through the fetch tool). (5) An arXiv preprint for the Barkley–Gaetz identity-permutation result, to date its write-up. (6) The journal of record for Chen–Hu (the news report and the arXiv DOI conflict). (7) A decision by the judging pass on whether positivity is part of the bullet.

judgement.why: The statement is the 1979 character conjecture for complex semisimple Lie algebras (values at 1 of KL polynomials as Verma multiplicities). The 1981 Beilinson–Bernstein and Brylinski–Kashiwara proofs answer it in full and are journal-published, long-accepted results, so whole/digested; Elias–Williamson (Annals) and BFN (Crelle) are further pre-snapshot complete proofs. Every post-snapshot event concerns a changed question — quantum, p-adic, modular, finite-group, sl_∞, stable-parabolic analogues, combinatorial invariance of the polynomials, the a-function, matroid KL polynomials, or Ext dimensions (Barkley–Gaetz–Lam, a different quantity than q=1 multiplicities) — so all are variant. Gabber–Joseph 1981 is unread and scored none. AI roles are answered per event: ChatGPT 5.5 Pro generated the Hjelle proof and Rethlas generated the Cheng–Liu counterexample (generated); LTV's 'generating conjectures, assisting with proof development' and Badalov's 'proof development' are assisted; the Barkley seminar event's proof is human (DeepMind's ML produced the conjecture in an earlier event), so none; Blundell et al. has no systems entry, so none.
judgement.doubts: Positivity of KL coefficients (the companion 1979 conjecture) is not named in the bullet; even if included, it was settled pre-snapshot by Elias–Williamson, so the outcome is unaffected. The group-level wording and the scope of weights in the 1981 proofs are unverified in the record. The bullet appears stale on the list.
